title: Heracles — Gods, heroes, and monsters
summary: Heracles performed the Twelve Labors — slaying the Nemean lion, the Hydra, and others — to atone for a madness-induced crime. This study profiles the figures at the myth's heart.
body:
Heracles performed the Twelve Labors — slaying the Nemean lion, the Hydra, and others — to atone for a madness-induced crime. He was the greatest hero of Greek myth, later worshipped as a god.

Myths are carried by persons — gods who are larger than human, heroes who are almost, monsters who embody what must be faced. In Heracles, each figure plays a role that reveals what the culture feared, honored, and desired. Viewed through a symbolic lens, Heracles is read for its images — what each figure and object stands for beneath the plot.

The figures of Heracles outlive their religion: they become metaphors the whole world now uses. A third sub-question asks how Heracles was visualized — in vase painting, sculpture, or temple relief. Related entries in this archive: Marduk and Hel.
